 Smoke Detectors:
 Common Reasons Smoke Detectors May Not Work
 Batteries are dead or missing.

 Sensing chamber is infested with small insects.
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Smoke Detectors:
 Proper Testing of a Smoke Detector
 The ʺtest button testʺ is not a true test of a smoke detector.

user_input: What are the common causes of wall cracks in houses, and how can they be concealed by homeowners during property inspections?
reference_contexts:

21
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Wall Cracks: 
 However, often they inadvertently conceal or hide defects.
 The following are usually concealed by the owners: wall cracks,

doors and windows.
 Therefore, you should make an effort to identify any possible
defects.
 Often a patched wall area will have a different surface texture

 The color of the paint may also be slightly different.

Guide
 Sloping Floors:
 In a typical house, floors are sufficiently level and any
sloping can be determined only by precise measuring.
 Do floors feel springy? A very springy floor indicates a
possible problem with the interior floor structure.
 You should look for cracks in all tile and marble floors.
 A continuous vertical crack that covers 3 sections of
marble or tile in the floor is always a Red Flag .

<2-hop>

20
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Wall Cracks:
 Cracks develop in the walls of houses for a number of
reasons.
 Wooden framing of the house may dry out and shrink
shortly after the house is built.
 Almost every house has a few hairline cracks caused by
shrinkage of wood.
 However, differential movement of the structure may occur,
caused by foundation movement or structural defects that
can cause significant wall cracking.
 When inspecting for cracking, pay particular attention to
common crack locations such as the corners of windows,
doors and the walls of rooms.
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Wall Cracks:
 Consciously look for crac ks behind curtains and on
ceilings throughout the house and make written notes
of the amount and severity of any cracking observed.
 A significant amount of diagonal cracking, large

 Homeowners commonly paint and patch homes for
aesthetic reasons prior to selling them.
reference: Wall cracks in houses can develop for several reasons, including the drying and shrinking of wooden framing shortly after construction, as well as differential movement of the structure due to foundation movement or structural defects. Homeowners often conceal these cracks by patching them, which may result in a different surface texture or color compared to the rest of the wall. Additionally, wallpaper may be used to redecorate walls, further hiding the cracks. During property inspections, it is crucial to look for cracks in common locations such as the corners of windows and doors, and to check behind curtains and on ceilings, making written notes of the amount and severity of any cracking observed.

user_input: What are the key requirements for building ventilation in properties, and how does proper drainage relate to hillside stability?
reference_contexts:
<1-hop>

9
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Proper Drainage, Building Ventilation, Hillside 
Instability, and Fills:
 Proper drainage of roof and yard areas is important because
water collecting near the house or underneath it can
aggravate existing soil problems.
 Expansive soils, when exposed to a large volume of water,
will swell to their maximum and then shrink dramatically
when dried again.
 Many foundations cannot tolerate these maximum shrinking
and swelling cycles.
 When a homeowner allows these conditions to exist, cracking
and settlement will result.
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Proper Drainage, Building Ventilation, Hillside 
Instability, and Fills:
 Loose fill ‐soil will sag and settle causing damage if they
are not kept well ‐drained.
 If water pools right next to a foundation, it can easily seep 
under the house, causing voids under the foundation, 
basement flooding, wood rot, damage to heat ducts, and 
swelling of wood floors.

<2-hop>

10
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Building Ventilation:
 The under‐floor space between the bottom of the floor joists and
the earth under any building (except space occupied by a
basement or cellar) shall be provided with ventilation openings
through foundation walls or exterior walls.
 The minimum net area of ventilation openings shall not be less
than 1 sq. ft. for each 150 sq. ft. of under ‐floor space area.
 The ventilation openings will be within 3 feet of each corner of
the building.
 Enclosed attics and enclosed rafter spaces formed where ceilings 
are applied directly to the underside of roof rafters shall have 
cross ventilation for each separate space by ventilating openings 
protected against the entrance of rain or snow.
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Building Ventilation:
 Ventilating openings shall be provided with a
corrosion‐resistant wire mesh that has 1/8 ‐inch
minimum and ¼‐inch maximum openings.
 The ventilation portals must be screened to prevent the
entrance of rodents and insects.
 The integrity of the ventilation portals should be
inspected and any damage reported.
reference: The key requirements for building ventilation in properties include providing ventilation openings through foundation walls or exterior walls, with a minimum net area of ventilation openings not less than 1 sq. ft. for each 150 sq. ft. of under-floor space area. Additionally, ventilating openings must be within 3 feet of each corner of the building and should be protected against the entrance of rain or snow. Proper drainage is crucial as it prevents water from pooling near the foundation, which can lead to soil problems that aggravate hillside instability. If water collects near the house, it can cause expansive soils to swell and shrink dramatically, leading to cracking and settlement of the foundation.

user_input: What are the red flags to look for during a property inspection regarding hazardous vegetation and sticking doors and windows?
reference_contexts:

23
Red Flags Property Inspection

 Sticking Doors and Windows:
 There are two things to look for when inspecting doors
and windows:
 1. sticking when you open or close them
 2. uneven spaces between doors and their frames
 These two symptoms usually mean movement of the walls
and floors have changed the shape of the window or

 Always open and close every door and window in the

Guide
 Sticking Doors and Windows:
 When you are inspecting a door, look at the spaces at the

 The door should resemble a long, narrow rectangle.
 Always look for signs that the door has been sawed or
sanded to make it fit the crooked frame.

<2-hop>

16
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Hazardous Vegetation:
 Dead or unhealthy trees should be identified, especially
those close to habitable structures.
 Poisonous plants, many of which are volunteer in a
house’s landscaping, can cause health problems.
 Some of these are: poison oak, poison sumac, poison ivy,
castor bean, and so on.
 Any of these located near the house should be
documented and disclosed.
Red Flags Property Inspection  
Guide
 Septic Systems:
 Whenever a house is not on the city sewer system, this house will 
usually have 1 of 2 different types of septic systems. 
 The first and most common type is a septic tank with a soil drain field.
 The second type is an aerator system that has sprinkler heads to 
disperse the processed wastewater.  
 Indications of a malfunctioning system include visible signs of seepage 
and a strong sewage smell.  
 A septic system needs to be at least 50 feet from a water well, 
underground cisterns, stream, lake, pond, sprinkler system, and/or 
swimming pool.
reference: During a property inspection, red flags to look for regarding hazardous vegetation include identifying dead or unhealthy trees, especially those close to habitable structures, and documenting poisonous plants such as poison oak, poison sumac, and poison ivy. Additionally, when inspecting doors and windows, one should check for sticking when opening or closing them and look for uneven spaces between doors and their frames, as these symptoms usually indicate movement of the walls and floors that have altered the shape of the door or window frame.
